content.title: City of Arvada Declares Stage 1 Drought: Mandatory Watering Restrictions Take Effect April 15
content.summary: The City of Arvada has declared Stage 1 drought conditions due to a dry winter and low snowpack, implementing mandatory watering restrictions starting April 15, 2026. All water customers must adhere to a two-day per week watering schedule and avoid watering during peak hours, with the goal of reducing overall water use by at least 20%. The City is also taking measures to conserve water in public spaces and golf courses while monitoring compliance with these restrictions.
content.body:
Arvada, CO – Following one of the driest winters on record in Colorado, warm temperatures, and historically low mountain snowpack levels, the City of Arvada has declared Stage 1 drought conditions and will implement mandatory watering restrictions effective April 15, 2026. The restrictions apply to all Arvada water customers, including residents, businesses, and City-managed properties.

The City’s Water Resources Administrator, Amy Willhite explained, “Maintaining a reliable water supply is a public health and safety priority for the City of Arvada. Restricting outdoor watering ensures we can continue to have the supply needed for drinking, cooking, cleaning, and other essential needs this year and in the future. These conservation measures protect our water supply through the current drought, and unknown future conditions. In a significant drought, it becomes the responsibility of our entire community to conserve water.”

## What Arvada Water Customers Need to Know

Beginning April 15, all Arvada water customers must follow a mandatory two-day per week watering schedule. Outdoor watering is not allowed from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

**Single-family residential**

- Even-numbered addresses: **Sunday and Thursday**
- Odd-numbered addresses: **Wednesday and Saturday**

**All others** (including multifamily and commercial)

- **Tuesday and Friday**, unless otherwise instructed

**Additional rules and best practices**

- Trees, shrubs, vegetable gardens, and flowers can be watered using a handheld hose or drip irrigation, outside of 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
- Do not waste water by letting it spray on concrete and asphalt or pool in gutters, streets, and alleys.
- Repair leaking sprinkler systems in a timely manner.
- Do not irrigate during rain or high winds.
- Use a hose nozzle with a shut-off valve when washing cars.
- Serve water at restaurants upon request.

The overall goal is to reduce water use across Arvada by at least 20%. 

## What the City is Doing

The City is taking steps to reduce water use and lead by example, including implementing a Drought Management Plan: 

- **Parks and public spaces:**Athletic fields, youth sports, and tree health are prioritized for water use. Turf grass watering will be reduced. This allows water to be reallocated to high-use, functional turf grass (such as athletic fields) and trees.
- **Golf courses:**West Woods and Lake Arbor Golf Courses will reduce water use through targeted irrigation, prioritizing greens and tees while allowing roughs and native areas to go dormant. The courses use state-of-the-art computerized irrigation systems to provide a high level of control over water use to ensure compliance with a 20% reduction in water use. Additional investments in wetting agents and moisture meters help soil moisture last longer and make informed decisions about watering respectively.
- **Irrigation technology:**The City continues to invest in computerized irrigation systems, weather stations, and water-efficient technology across all parks and public facilities to apply the right amount of water at the right time.
- **Alternative water sources:**Arvada maximizes the use of non-potable water sources, including ditch water, to reduce pressure on potable water sources. Some of the City’s athletic fields (Long Lake, Stenger, and Lutz), as well as West Woods Golf Club use non-potable water sources for irrigation.
- **Monitoring and enforcement:**The City will actively monitor water use and water waste. Violations of the mandatory watering restrictions may result in fines as outlined in the Arvada City Code.

## Resources and Water-Saving Tips

Current information, including more details on watering restrictions, drought conditions, and how to conserve water are available at [**arvadaco.gov/drought**](//arvadaco.gov/drought)**.** The City has a variety of resources to help customers reduce water use: 

- [**Resource Central**](http://resourcecentral.org) free and low-cost programs to help save water outdoors.
- [**Outdoor watering tips**](https://www.arvadaco.gov/597) provide practical guidance for improving irrigation efficiency and maintaining a healthy landscape with less water.
- [**EyeOnWater**](https://www.arvadaco.gov/835) is a free tool being rolled out to customers to track their water use in near-real time, set leak alerts, and identify unusual usage patterns. 
  - This technology is still being installed and not yet available to all customers. If your water meter has a black plastic lid you are likely able to join the program.
- [**Indoor leak detection tips**](https://www.arvadaco.gov/1505) can help find and fix leaks that can waste water.

## Background on Arvada Water Supply and Drought Conditions

The City of Arvada receives the majority of its raw water supply from Denver Water. All of Arvada’s water supply is stored in reservoirs that are filled and replenished largely with melted mountain snowpack. While reservoir storage is relatively healthy, and Arvada has a robust water supply during normal years, conserving now ensures that we maintain a healthy supply and can recover from low-supply and drought conditions more effectively.
